FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
Traffic signals exist mainly to direct and regulate traffic, and they are installed at intersections and other places where the flow of traffic must be interrupted [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
Standard three-color signals are used mainly to stop and release traffic at locations with considerable conflict between vehicle movements [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
On a red light you must stop at the stop line, or before entering the crosswalk if there is no stop line, or before entering the intersection if there is neither, and you must remain stopped until the signal turns green [A01].
Why it matters: the stopping point has a three-step fallback: stop line, then crosswalk, then intersection.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
After stopping on red you may turn right unless a sign prohibits it, and you must yield to all pedestrians and all vehicles while making that turn [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
After stopping on red you may also turn left from a one-way street onto another one-way street whose traffic moves to the left, unless a sign prohibits that turn [A01].
Why it matters: the left turn on red exists only between two one-way streets.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A01
A yellow light warns that red is about to appear, so you should avoid entering the intersection on yellow, and you must never enter the intersection after the red light is shown [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0039]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A02
A green light means go straight or turn unless signs prohibit the turn, and you must yield to all pedestrians and vehicles already in the intersection [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A02
Lighted arrows are sometimes used to control turns from a specific lane, and a red arrow or a yellow arrow carries the same meaning as a red or yellow light for that lane [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A02
A green arrow has the same meaning as a green light for its lane, but you must turn or proceed only in the direction the arrow points [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0040]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A03
Combination signals pair arrows with standard lights to control every lane, the colors and arrows keep their usual meanings, and when a green arrow is lighted you must move only in the direction it indicates [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A03
Flashing signals are sometimes used to warn of danger, a flashing red signal has the same meaning as a stop sign and a stop sign is also posted there, and a flashing yellow signal means proceed only with caution [A03].
Why it matters: flashing red equals a stop sign; flashing yellow equals caution, not stop.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A03
When a regular traffic signal shows flashing lights, the flashing red and flashing yellow carry the same meanings as the separate flashing signals [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A03
Lane control signals are mounted over the lane they govern and set the direction of travel in a lane that carries one direction at some times and the opposite direction at others [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A03
A red X over a lane means you must not use that lane because traffic in the opposite direction is using it [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0041]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A04
A green arrow lane control signal means you may use that lane, and a steady yellow X means you must move out of the lane because it is about to carry traffic in the opposite direction [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A04
When the yellow X lane control signal is flashing, you may use that lane only while preparing to turn left [A04].
Why it matters: steady yellow X means leave the lane; flashing yellow X means left turns only.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A04
Pedestrian signals control only pedestrian movements and use the lighted words WALK and DON'T WALK together with the symbols of a walking person and an upraised palm [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A04
A steady DON'T WALK or upraised palm means pedestrians must not enter the roadway toward the signal, while a flashing one means no one may start crossing but anyone already crossing may continue to the nearest sidewalk, traffic island or safety zone [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A04
A steady WALK or walking person means pedestrians may cross toward the signal, and a flashing WALK or walking person is sometimes used to warn of a possible conflict between pedestrians and vehicles [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0042]

Misconceptions: a yellow light is a warning to avoid entering, not a signal to speed up, and entering after red is always prohibited; a left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto a one-way street; a flashing red signal is a stop sign, while a flashing yellow only asks for caution; a steady yellow X means get out of the lane, but a flashing yellow X allows the lane for a left turn; a flashing DON'T WALK lets pedestrians already in the street finish crossing.

Mnemonics: Stop line, then crosswalk, then intersection for the red stop point; flashing red is a stop sign, flashing yellow is caution; red X no, green arrow yes, yellow X leave, flashing yellow X left turn only.

Glossary: stop line (the white line marking the red-light stopping point); lighted arrow (a signal that governs one lane's turning movement); combination signal (arrows and standard lights working together); lane control signal (an overhead X or arrow that sets a reversible lane's direction); upraised palm (the pedestrian symbol for do not walk).

Dynamic facts: none; signal meanings are national conventions printed as stable knowledge in this edition.
